Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Decades ago, Kwame's life fractured during the sudden collapse of his homeland, when soldiers at a flooded checkpoint opened fire without warning. He had frozen when the guards barked orders to fall to their knees, and in that suspended terror, his mind simply shut off, leaving him feeling detached from the violence unfolding around him. What remained were not full narratives but sharp, unblinking snapshots: the glint of rifle barrels, the dust pluming over cracked earth, the cold command echoing in his ears. As he resettled in the United States, built a career in software engineering, and married his wife, those fragments did not fade. Instead, they settled into a quiet, emotionless recall; when they surfaced, Kwame could describe the scene with clinical detachment, as though it had happened to a stranger, yet the images would lock onto his vision without warning. Now seventy-seven, Kwame spent his days in a dimly lit home office where lines of code occupied his screen and his attention. The transition to remote work had once felt like a mercy, but the isolation only sharpened his vulnerability. When a local documentary aired footage of a border crackdown or a project manager emailed directives to assign urgent debugging tasks, those familiar trauma-related events and authority commands pressed against his ribs, instantly pulling the old visual memories back into focus. He could not help but see the same rigid posture in a manager's typed instructions, and the snapshot images would flood his mind, cold and unyielding. To keep the pictures from paralyzing him, Kwame developed a rigid routine of staying indoors and declining social invitations. He would avoid going out to the corner pharmacy and shut down conversations with colleagues, instead burying his thoughts in complex algorithms and technical manuals. The numbness of those recalled images, however, only deepened his retreat. Because he remembered the event as a series of frozen photographs rather than a lived experience, Kwame believed he had to keep his mind perpetually occupied, fearing that a single quiet moment would let the fragments take over. That relentless mental distraction, in turn, stripped the memories of any chance to soften; without processing, the snapshots remained bright and unyielding, which made his nervous system hypersensitive to the slightest hint of coercion. The more he avoided people and isolated himself, the less he had to correct his assumptions, so when a client suddenly raised their voice on a video call or a delivery driver knocked at his door, the sight of an imposing figure would instantly reignite the original command. In the beginning, the silence of his study felt like safety. Over time, the quiet only amplified the static in his head, and he found himself pacing the floorboards at three in the morning, tracing the same digital architectures until his eyes burned and the old faces in his mind finally blinked out. Over months, the habits hardened into necessity. His wife noticed how he would stare past her while she spoke, his eyes fixed on some invisible screen, and how he stopped attending their grandson's graduation because he could not bear the risk of strangers' voices in a crowded hall. The software projects still required him, but he completed them with a brittle efficiency, counting lines of code under his breath to keep the quiet at bay. He would rewrite functions three times, convinced that a misplaced semicolon might somehow summon the checkpoint guards. What finally brought him to the clinic was a Tuesday morning when a simple voice-mail reminder from a vendor made him drop his coffee cup, his chest seizing with that familiar, unreal detachment. He was terrified that the past had finally caught up to him, that the snapshots would never stop flashing, and that he would be forced to face the authority he had spent years outrunning. He hoped, however faintly, that someone might help him untangle the pictures from the present without asking him to surrender the only routine that kept them at bay.
